items.title: First imaged black hole
items.claim: The Event Horizon Telescope released the first image of a supermassive black hole in 2019. Which one?

options.text: Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way
The black hole at the centre of M87, around 53 million light-years away
A solar-mass black hole in Cygnus

items.reveal_title: M87* came first; Sagittarius A* followed in 2022
items.reveal:
EHT's M87* image released 10 April 2019; Sagittarius A* image released 12 May 2022. M87* is roughly 6.5 billion solar masses; Sagittarius A* is around 4 million.

EHT combines radio telescopes on multiple continents to create an Earth-sized aperture.
items.why: Imaging the largest objects in the universe required a planet-sized synthetic instrument.

items.title: How long photons take to escape the Sun
items.claim: A photon generated in the Sun's core takes how long, on average, to reach the surface?
items.reveal_title: Tens of thousands of years through a dense plasma
items.reveal:
The radiative zone is so opaque that photons random-walk outward. Mitalas and Sills (1992) modelled the escape time at about 10,000 to 170,000 years depending on assumptions.

Once free, the photon reaches Earth in about 8 minutes 20 seconds.
items.why: The dramatic part of a photon's journey is hidden inside its source, not its trip across space.

items.title: The first confirmed exoplanets
items.claim: The first exoplanets confirmed orbited an unusual host. What was it?

options.text: A pulsar (PSR B1257+12), with the discovery announced in 1992

items.reveal_title: Pulsar planets, three years before 51 Pegasi b
items.reveal:
Aleksander Wolszczan and Dale Frail confirmed planets around the millisecond pulsar PSR B1257+12 in 1992.

Mayor and Queloz's 51 Pegasi b (1995) was the first around a sunlike star and won the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics.
items.why: Public memory often centres on the second discovery if the first occurs in an exotic setting.
